questions.title: 1. Timely Injury Reporting
questions.text: Work-related injuries and incidents are reported internally to the appropriate person immediately or as soon as practicable after they occur, regardless of their apparent severity.
questions.implication: Delays in reporting can slow care coordination and early claim response.
questions.prompt: When was the last injury reported, and how much time passed before the right people were notified?
questions.validation: Average time from injury to supervisor notification and carrier/TPA reporting; % reported within target timeframe.
questions.improve: Establish a clear expectation that all injuries and incidents are reported internally the same day they occur, regardless of severity, and confirm that supervisors and employees know exactly who to notify.

questions.title: 2. Supervisor Response and Incident Investigation
questions.text: When an injury or incident occurs, supervisors respond promptly, document what happened, and investigate the contributing factors — not simply who was at fault.
questions.implication: Without a consistent response and investigation, contributing factors may remain unresolved and similar incidents may recur.
questions.prompt: What does a supervisor do after an incident, and how do you confirm that contributing factors were addressed?
questions.validation: % of incidents investigated within target timeframe; completeness of root-cause and corrective-action documentation.
questions.improve: Build a simple, repeatable incident-investigation process so supervisors document what happened and identify contributing factors, not just who was at fault.

questions.title: 3. Medical Direction and Provider Coordination
questions.text: Employees and supervisors know where an injured employee should receive appropriate medical care, and the organization coordinates the initial treatment process.
questions.implication: Gaps in coordination can make it harder to align treatment, work restrictions, and recovery with the employee's actual duties.
questions.prompt: How do you coordinate appropriate care and share job duties with the provider when an injury occurs?
questions.validation: % of cases using designated/appropriate providers where permitted; time from injury to coordinated medical follow-up.
questions.improve: Make sure employees and supervisors know, in advance, where injured employees should go for initial treatment, and coordinate that first medical visit directly rather than leaving it to the employee.

questions.title: 4. Return-to-Work Management
questions.text: The organization actively identifies meaningful transitional or modified-duty work to help injured employees return safely and productively as soon as medically appropriate.
questions.implication: When suitable work is not consistently identified, an employee may spend more time away from work.
questions.prompt: When an employee has work restrictions, how do you identify and offer suitable work? What happened in the most recent case?
questions.validation: Days from injury to modified-duty offer; % of eligible injured employees returned to transitional duty; duration of modified duty.
questions.improve: Create a standing list of modified or transitional-duty tasks so a return-to-work offer is ready before it's needed, rather than improvised after each injury.

questions.title: 5. Claims Oversight and Reserve Management
questions.text: Open workers' compensation claims are reviewed regularly with the broker, carrier, claims administrator, or other appropriate parties to monitor progress, barriers, and financial exposure.
questions.implication: Infrequent claim review can leave barriers, next actions, or significant reserve changes without timely management attention.
questions.prompt: Who reviews open claims, next actions, and significant reserve changes with the carrier or claims administrator?
questions.validation: Open-claim review cadence; age of open claims; time since last carrier/TPA update; significant reserve changes; documented reserve discussions and escalation actions.
questions.improve: Put a recurring claims-review meeting on the calendar with your broker, carrier, or claims administrator so open claims, reserve changes, and stalled cases get regular visibility.

questions.title: 6. Safety Leadership and Employee Engagement
questions.text: Leaders and supervisors consistently reinforce safe work practices, involve employees in identifying risks, and hold themselves and others accountable for safety performance.
questions.implication: If concerns are raised but corrective actions are not followed through, preventable hazards may persist.
questions.prompt: How do employees raise safety concerns, and how does leadership confirm that corrective actions were completed?
questions.validation: Frequency of safety leadership touchpoints; employee participation; closure rate for identified safety actions.
questions.improve: Give supervisors a simple, recurring way to reinforce safety expectations and involve employees directly in identifying hazards, rather than relying on posters or annual training alone.

questions.title: 7. Near-Miss Reporting and Continuous Improvement
questions.text: Employees are encouraged to report near misses and unsafe conditions, and the organization reviews those reports to prevent future injuries.
questions.implication: Missed near-miss lessons can leave a hazard in place until a more serious event occurs.
questions.prompt: What happened after the last near miss was reported, and how was the lesson shared?
questions.validation: Near-misses reported per period; % investigated; corrective-action closure rate and recurrence tracking.
questions.improve: Create an easy, low-friction way for employees to report near misses and unsafe conditions, and make sure those reports are actually reviewed and acted on.

questions.title: 8. Payroll Reporting and Classification Accuracy
questions.text: Payroll, employee duties, classifications, overtime, and other remuneration information are reviewed for accuracy before being reported to the workers' compensation carrier or payroll provider.
questions.implication: Inaccurate payroll reporting or classifications can contribute to audit adjustments and unexpected premium changes.
questions.prompt: How do you check payroll reports and job classifications before they become an audit issue?
questions.validation: Audit exceptions; classification corrections; payroll variance; reconciliation accuracy and timeliness.
questions.improve: Add a regular check of payroll, job classifications, and overtime reporting before it goes to the carrier or payroll provider, to catch errors before they affect premium.

questions.title: 9. Broker Strategy and Market Story
questions.text: The organization works with its insurance advisor throughout the policy year — not only at renewal — to review losses, operational changes, risk-improvement efforts, and the organization's underwriting story.
questions.implication: Without early renewal planning, the employer may have less time to address underwriting questions and explain operational improvements.
questions.prompt: What does your broker review with you before renewal beyond obtaining quotes?
questions.validation: Documented stewardship and claim-review meetings; pre-renewal planning cadence; broker involvement in carrier/TPA escalations; completion of underwriting action items.
questions.improve: Move the relationship with your insurance advisor from a once-a-year renewal conversation to a year-round one that includes loss reviews, risk-improvement planning, and underwriting strategy.

questions.title: 10. Leadership Accountability and Continuous Performance Review
questions.text: Leadership regularly reviews workers' compensation performance and assigns clear responsibility for improving the operational behaviors that influence injuries, claims, and insurance costs.
questions.implication: Improvements may stall when no one owns the action or checks whether it was completed.
questions.prompt: Who owns each improvement action, and how does leadership check that it was completed?
questions.validation: Quarterly review of CCB metrics; documented owners, due dates, and completion of corrective actions.
questions.improve: Assign clear ownership for workers' compensation performance and put a recurring leadership review on the calendar so these behaviors are actively managed, not just assumed.
